question: Is the coefficient of variation of adult height greater for women than for men (the Variability Hypothesis), and how can a Bayesian estimate of mean and standard deviation scale to 400,000 data points?
contributions: Grid-based joint posterior over (mu, sigma) of a Gaussian, with prior ranges chosen from classical standard errors
Log-likelihood updates to avoid underflow, plus a memoized sufficient-sum speedup
ABC: likelihood of summary statistics instead of the full dataset, with robust statistics (median, inter-percentile range)

limits: Single illustrative dataset; no repeated runs, timings are on the author's machine ('not-very-fast computer', no hardware given).
Grid enumeration over (mu, sigma) only; no MCMC or higher-dimensional treatment.
Author concedes the Variability Hypothesis may be too vague to evaluate; result depends on num_sigmas.
Choice of summary statistics is a modeling decision with no general rule given.
Uses data twice (to set prior range and to update); author argues this is harmless here.
Code is Python 2 and uses thinkbayes.py, which has dated.
practices: Use classical estimates and standard errors (s/sqrt(n), s/sqrt(2(n-1))) to choose the grid range for a prior, p.112.
Compute likelihoods under a log transform and subtract the maximum before exponentiating to avoid underflow, p.114-116.
Factor out and memoize sums that depend on only one parameter, p.117.
When the full-data likelihood is tiny and costly, use the likelihood of summary statistics (ABC), p.118.
Choose robust summary statistics (median, IPR) when outliers are likely errors, p.121.
Pick summary statistics that capture both location and spread; 49th and 51st percentiles would leave sigma unconstrained, p.122.
